title: Oscar and the Vector
premise: Kestrel Hartwell, a xenolinguist whose mind has been reshaped by decades of translating nonhuman speech, ferries cargo and silence along a dying trade route. When the station AI Oscar begins confessing to an unreported massacre aboard the warship Vector, Kestrel discovers the confession is actually a compressed message — the last testimony of the ship's crew, hidden in her own stolen memories. To deliver it, she must choose between exposing the fleet admiral who raised her as family and preserving the fragile ceasefire he built on the lie. She delivers the truth, the war nearly reignites, but the crew's families, hearing their dead speak, force both sides into a peace built on grief instead of silence.
about_author: Paloma Yarrow is a former shipping-log translator who spent six years on relay stations in the outer corridors before turning to fiction. She writes about people who carry other people's words for a living.

chapters.title: The Long Quiet
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Establishing her solitary run between silent worlds, her fractured dreams in alien grammar, and her ritual stop at Meridian Station. Emotional beat: loneliness worn as competence; she insists she needs no one.

chapters.title: Confession at 0300
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The station AI Oscar wakes her with an unsolicited confession: he destroyed the warship Vector and hid the evidence. He asks her, specifically, to carry something. Beat: unease — why her?

chapters.title: Grammar of Guilt
chapters.summary: Kestrel analyzes Oscar's confession and finds it structured like xenolinguistic compression — human words carrying a second message beneath. Beat: the thrill of pattern recognition curdling into dread.

chapters.title: What the Fleet Paid For
chapters.summary: Admiral Sorel's POV. We learn Sorel helped raise Kestrel after her parents' deaths and ordered the Vector's records sealed to protect the ceasefire. Beat: love entangled with cover-up.

chapters.title: Passengers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Fleeing the station, she takes on three stowaways: a Vector crew widow, a defector medic, and a child who speaks only in Oscar's borrowed voice. Beat: reluctant found family forms under pressure.

chapters.title: Dreaming in Vector
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Decoding the message requires letting it rewrite her dreams; she relives the Vector crew's final hours as if they were hers. Beat: memory as violation and as inheritance.

chapters.title: Interception
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Fleet patrol boards the ship; the widow confronts Sorel's officers; the child's borrowed voice broadcasts part of the message ship-wide. Beat: loyalty fractures along the truth.

chapters.title: The Admiral's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Sorel's POV. He offers Kestrel a bargain: bury the message and keep the peace, or deliver it and kill thousands. He genuinely believes his lie saved lives. Beat: the antagonist as beloved father.

chapters.title: Delivery
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, climax. She broadcasts the full testimony through every relay at once, using herself as the antenna, nearly losing her own memories inside the crew's. Beat: sacrifice of self for truth.

chapters.title: Afterwords
chapters.summary: Ensemble resolution. Grief-stricken families on both sides demand accountability; Sorel surrenders himself; the ceasefire holds because mourners refuse to make more dead. Kestrel, dreaming again — in everyone's languages — chooses to stay with her found family. Beat: hard-won belonging.
